q: who were the most influential women in the early history of computing
famous women in computer science history
female mathematicians who contributed to computing
a: The early history of computing was shaped profoundly by several brilliant women whose contributions laid the foundation for modern computer science. Ada Lovelace (1815–1852) is widely recognized as the world's first programmer. She collaborated with Charles Babbage on his Analytical Engine and wrote what is considered the first algorithm intended for machine execution, along with visionary insights about computing beyond mere number-crunching. Grace Hopper (1906–1992) was a rear admiral in the U.S. Navy and a pioneering computer scientist who developed the first compiler, the A-0 System, and was instrumental in creating COBOL, one of the first high-level programming languages. She also popularized the term 'debugging' after literally removing a moth from the Harvard Mark II computer. The six ENIAC programmers — Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Meltzer, Fran Bilas, and Ruth Lichterman — were recruited during World War II to program the Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer, the first general-purpose electronic digital computer. Working without programming languages or manuals, they manually configured the machine by setting switches and routing cables to compute artillery trajectories. Their work was largely unrecognized for decades until their induction into the Women in Technology Hall of Fame in 1997. Hedy Lamarr (1914–2000), the famous Hollywood actress, co-invented frequency-hopping spread spectrum technology during World War II, originally designed to prevent torpedo jamming. This invention later became a foundation for Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and GPS. Other influential figures include Katherine Johnson (1918–2020), the NASA mathematician whose orbital calculations were critical to the success of Project Mercury and the Apollo moon landing; her story was featured in the film 'Hidden Figures'. Dorothy Vaughan (1910–2008) was NASA's first Black manager and an expert in FORTRAN programming. Jean Bartik (one of the ENIAC programmers) later worked on early computers including UNIVAC I. Sister Mary Kenneth Keller (1913–1985) became the first American woman to earn a PhD in computer science in 1965 and contributed to the development of the BASIC programming language. Dame Stephanie Shirley founded a pioneering software company in the 1960s that employed mostly women. Frances Allen (1932–2020) was the first woman to win the Turing Award for her work on optimizing compilers. These women overcame significant gender and racial barriers to make foundational contributions to computing, and their legacies continue to inspire new generations of computer scientists.
